welcome: The SOBRI Cork House is an extension of SOBRI, a Porto lifestyle brand built around cork, one of the most amazing natural raw materials. We see the house as a gallery, a showroom, or simply a comfortable place to spend a few days.
Everything in this space was chosen to feel natural and comfortable, combining cork with wood and steel. It is made in Portugal, and the whole atmosphere reflects what SOBRI stands for.
Feel free to explore our home, and enjoy. Below are the places we love in Porto. If you want to know something specific, just ask us.

cellars.label: Port wine cellars
cellars.intro: Visiting the Port wine cellars should be near the top of your list. There are 16 cellars in Vila Nova de Gaia, just across the river, and the tours are similar in all of them. These are the ones we suggest.

dates.name: São João
dates.text: Porto's biggest party. The whole city stays out all night: grilled sardines on every corner, pots of basil, plastic hammers, and fireworks over the Douro at midnight. If you're here, don't go to bed early.

places.name: Cervejaria Brasão
places.tagline: The best francesinha, from a wood-fired oven
places.review: We start with the star of Porto's food, the famous francesinha. Many restaurants claim to make the best one. For us (and many others), the best comes from our neighbours at Brasão, a cosy, well-designed space that has mastered the recipe in a wood-fired oven.

places.name: Casa Guedes
places.tagline: The most famous sandwich in town
places.review: A simple, inexpensive menu with one of Porto's stars: the roast pork sandwich with queijo da Serra, the soft cheese from the mountains. Mr. César opened it in 1987 and still brings his contagious good mood. There is always a queue, and it is always worth the wait. Have it with a beer.

places.name: Venham Mais 5
places.tagline: Another sandwich you don't want to miss
places.review: By now you may think Porto only offers bread, cheese and meat. Sorry, but Venham Mais 5 had to be on this list. Its famous sandwiches come with steak and queijo da Serra, and it is close to Casa Guedes, so you can try one in each place.

places.name: Taberna de Santo António
places.review: Small space, huge quality. Few places cook Portuguese food like this: Dona Hermínia makes the classic dishes as if our mother or grandmother made them. Try the rissóis too. You won't be disappointed.

places.name: Pontual
places.review: Right in front of the Cork House. A simple snack bar with cheap, tasty food, perfect for a quick late meal and a taste of classic Porto service. Try the bôla, a sweet bread filled with Portuguese cured meats, made every day until 2am.

places.name: Puro 4050
places.review: An original concept where mozzarella is the star, served in many forms with grilled vegetables, Italian cured meats and more.

places.name: Shiko
places.review:
The first Japanese place in Porto to offer more than sushi, created by chef Ruy Leão, a true expert in Japanese food. Small plates rule the menu. Try the okonomiyaki, a Japanese pancake with seafood and bacon.

The space is small and intimate, so book ahead.

places.name: LSD
places.review: A modern space in Largo de São Domingos, in the heart of the city. Light meals at lunch, and contemporary, international cooking at dinner.

places.name: Reitoria
places.review: A wine bar and steak house in a beautifully restored 19th-century building, with a balcony lined with olive trees. The menu is short and built around different cuts of meat.

places.name: Nola Kitchen
places.review: Right next to the Cork House. Tasty organic food with no processed ingredients, and a small market, all in a relaxed, minimalist space.
places.address: Praça Dona Filipa de Lencastre 25, Porto

places.name: Boa Bao
places.tagline: A trip to an Asian market
places.review: The red neon at the door invites you into a place that makes you travel. Start with an exotic cocktail at the lobby bar, then sit down and imagine you're in an Asian market. Light pours in through the glass ceiling across several rooms, fed by two kitchens.

places.name: Cantinho do Avillez
places.review: José Avillez is one of Portugal's most renowned chefs, with two Michelin stars. His first Porto restaurant is friendly, cosy and relaxed, with contemporary cooking inspired by Portuguese traditions.

places.name: Curb
places.review: It may sound like an exaggeration, but Curb has the best burgers in Porto, maybe in the world. High-quality beef, bread baked in house every day, and only 120 burgers a day, so they sell out daily.

places.name: Elemento
places.review: The first fire-dining restaurant in Portugal. No gas, no electricity: oak, orange, apple and olive wood cook fresh, seasonal ingredients. Chef and owner Ricardo Dias Ferreira believes cooking is going back to its roots.

places.name: O Carniceiro
places.review:
Inside the Zero Box Lodge, a red neon sign leads you down the corridor. The open kitchen, bar and library make it a box of surprises, with books picked by writer Gonçalo M. Tavares and colourful, smoking cocktails at the bar.

The meat of the day sits in a shop window: you choose, and they cook it in the open kitchen. It isn't a steakhouse, though. The menu is about sharing plates.
places.address: Rua Ateneu Comercial do Porto 13, Porto

places.name: O Lusitano
places.review: Run by Rosa and Zé, next to the Matosinhos fish market, on a street with dozens of fish restaurants. This is exactly where we like to have fresh fish for lunch on a sunny Sunday.

places.name: Mistu
places.review: It used to be a locksmith, then a bar, and now it takes you around the world's kitchens. Chef Rui Mingatos mixes Asia, South America and a Portuguese touch: white fish ceviche, oysters, sea bass with green asparagus, Uruguayan picanha with chimichurri. There is a signature cocktail bar too.
places.address: Rua do Comércio do Porto 161, Porto

places.name: Manna Porto
places.tagline: Eat and meditate · breakfast and lunch
places.review: A peaceful place with local, organic, seasonal food. Breakfasts, snacks and light vegan and vegetarian meals, plus a bright room with large windows for yoga and meditation classes.

places.name: DOP
places.review: One of the best restaurants in Porto. Chef Rui Paula reinvents traditional Portuguese cooking, à la carte or as a tasting menu. It won't leave you indifferent.
places.address: Palácio das Artes, Largo de São Domingos 18, Porto

places.name: Passeio das Virtudes
places.review: A special place for SOBRI: many of the ideas in the brand's DNA were born here. Perfect for a late afternoon, watching the sunset over the Douro with a beer and a good conversation. You'll find all kinds of people, from jugglers to office workers, lots of dogs, and new friends.

places.name: Jardins do Palácio de Cristal
places.tagline: Romantic gardens with a river view
places.review: Eight hectares of romantic gardens, designed in the 19th century by German landscape architect Émile David. The Crystal Palace itself is gone, but the gardens hold century-old Japanese trees, a fragrant rose garden and a viewpoint over the Douro.
places.address: Rua de Dom Manuel II, Porto

places.name: Jardim do Morro
places.review: On the Gaia side of the river, next to the upper deck of the D. Luís I bridge. An amazing lookout over the historic centre, and at night the view of Porto is charming.
places.address: Avenida da República, Vila Nova de Gaia

places.name: Jardim Botânico
places.review: Dating back to 1837, Porto's botanical garden has rare and exotic plants, greenhouses, lakes and centuries-old trees across 4.4 hectares in Campo Alegre. There is a curious cactus and succulent garden, and old leafy trees that are perfect for a picnic.

places.name: Fundação Serralves
places.review: A cultural institution with a contemporary vision of art and landscape. It has one of the largest and most beautiful gardens in Porto, with grazing animals, a contemporary art museum and the Serralves house, where exhibitions and concerts take place. Art installations often pop up in the gardens.
places.address: Rua Dom João de Castro 210, Porto

places.name: Parque da Cidade
places.tagline: A park that reaches the ocean
places.review: The largest urban park in Portugal: 83 hectares running all the way to the Atlantic, which is rare anywhere in the world. Designed by Sidónio Pardal, with stone walls and paths that give it a countryside feel. Perfect for exploring on a sunny day.

places.name: Casa da Música
places.review: Built when Porto was European Capital of Culture in 2001, designed by Dutch architect Rem Koolhaas. Today it is an icon of contemporary architecture in Portugal. Check the programme and catch a concert if you can.

places.name: Leixões Cruise Terminal
places.review: Designed by Luís Pedro Silva and opened in 2015, it won ArchDaily's Building of the Year 2017 for public architecture. From afar it makes you curious, and up close its white hexagonal tiles are overwhelming.

places.name: Casa de Chá da Boa Nova
places.review: One of Álvaro Siza Vieira's first projects (1958). As soon as you walk in, the windows open onto the horizon. Today it is a two-Michelin-star restaurant run by chef Rui Paula, but even if you don't eat here, the visit is worth it.
places.address: Avenida da Liberdade 1681, Leça da Palmeira

places.name: Rua do Almada
places.review:
The Cork House is on this street. It was the first street built outside the old city wall, in 1761, and the first in Porto with sidewalks. It was once known as the hardware street: not long ago more than 60 hardware shops were here.

Many buildings were abandoned for years and are now being restored. That is how the SOBRI Cork House was born.

places.name: Miguel Bombarda
places.review: Known as the art district for its many galleries with free entry, on Rua Miguel Bombarda and the streets around it, like Rua do Rosário and Rua do Breyner. There are also concept stores, studios and ateliers. If you want unique design pieces and a taste of Porto's creative scene, this is a must.

places.name: Bainharia, Mercadores, Aldas
places.review: Get lost in Porto's oldest alleys, where you can feel the soul of downtown. Narrow streets, mostly lived in by people born and raised here. A completely different reality from Rua Mouzinho da Silveira, just a few metres away.

places.name: Rua Escura
places.review: One of the oldest streets in Porto, first recorded in 1301 as Rua Nova and renamed Rua Escura, the dark street, around 1404. Locals say the name comes from the tall medieval buildings that once blocked the sunlight.

places.name: Rua de Cedofeita
places.tagline: From the medieval port to the upper city
places.review: An 840-metre street from Praça Carlos Alberto to Rua da Boavista that once linked the medieval river port to the upper city. Its name comes from the Church of São Martinho de Cedofeita, from the 6th century, and the Latin 'cito facta', meaning 'made early'. Many of its 18th and 19th-century buildings are protected.

places.name: Rua da Torrinha
places.review: Antiques, furniture and home decor, vintage clothes and accessories. For a sweet tooth there are brigadeiros, brownies and cakes, and for something more filling, Afonso serves burgers and one of the best francesinhas in town.

places.name: Foz Velha
places.tagline: Where the river meets the sea
places.review:
Between the Douro and the sea, Foz Velha sometimes feels like a separate city. In the 19th century wealthy families built summer houses here, making it one of the city's noblest areas. Walk its narrow streets and centuries-old houses, and say good afternoon to the fishermen tending their boats.

Renting a bike in Ribeira and riding along the river to Foz is a delight.

places.name: Praia do Senhor da Pedra
places.review: A 20-minute drive from Porto, Miramar beach has a chapel built on a rock in 1686. Locals say it's the only church with its back to the sea. We can't confirm that, but the scenery is incredible, especially at high tide, when the chapel sits in the middle of the water.
places.address: Alameda do Senhor da Pedra, Gulpilhares

places.name: Graça Rooftop
places.review: On the 4th floor of the Rivoli Cinema Hostel, relaxed and cosy, with sofas, plants and a view of the cathedral and Clérigos tower. On Sunday evenings there is bossa nova and Brazilian barbecue. A delight.

places.name: Aduela
places.tagline: A glass of wine that lasts all night
places.review: Next to the Carlos Alberto theatre, one of the favourite terraces of Porto's international crowd for a glass of wine at the end of the day, which often lasts into the night.

places.name: Catraio
places.review: One of the first places to serve craft beer in Porto. New beers from around the world arrive every month.

places.name: Capela Incomum
places.tagline: A wine bar in a chapel
places.review: A wine bar in a 19th-century chapel, altar included. In winter it feels like a living room, and in summer the terrace is where you want to be. A good selection of Portuguese wines and snacks at fair prices.

places.name: Kiosk Mompilher
places.review: A wooden kiosk from the early 20th century at the top of Rua da Picaria, protected since 1996. It has no indoor space, so it opens only when the weather allows, with an airy terrace for a drink.

places.name: Maus Hábitos
places.review: On a 4th floor across from the Coliseu, mixing music, art, food, drinks and parties for a mixed crowd. The place for anything experimental: concerts, fado, cinema and gatherings.

places.name: Pipa Velha
places.review: One of Porto's most legendary bars, ideal for a beer, a glass of wine or a good whisky with Portuguese snacks.

places.name: Plano B
places.review: Two floors: big sofas upstairs to sit and talk, and two dance floors downstairs. Theme parties, a varied crowd and music until 6am.

places.name: Gare
places.review: An underground club in an old railway tunnel for techno lovers, with one of the best sound systems in the city and top national and international DJs every month.

places.name: Cálem
places.review: A world reference, with around 313,000 visitors a year. The interactive museum takes you from the Douro soil to the grapes and aromas, and the guided tour ends with a white and a tawny Port. Combine it with a fado show for the perfect ending.
places.address: Avenida Diogo Leite 344, Vila Nova de Gaia

places.name: Sandeman
places.review: In an 1811 granite building facing the historic centre across the river. The museum tells the story of George Sandeman, a young Scot who started selling wine in London in 1790, through paintings, old bottles and more.
places.address: Largo Miguel Bombarda 47, Vila Nova de Gaia

places.name: WOW, World of Wine
places.tagline: Wine, cork and the story of Porto
places.review: Opened in 2020 in Gaia, WOW covers the history of Portuguese wine, the ritual of glasses and the cork industry, plus the city's story and the north's textile and fashion industries. Seven museum experiences, twelve restaurants and bars, a wine school, shops and a terrace with a great view of Porto.
places.address: Rua do Choupelo 39, Vila Nova de Gaia

places.name: Trindade car park
places.review: The easiest place to leave a car near the house. A covered car park run by STCP, right at Trindade, open day and night, a short walk from the door. Street parking around Rua do Almada is scarce and paid, so this saves a lot of circling.

places.name: Trindade metro lockers
places.tagline: Self-service lockers inside the station · 6:00 to 01:00
places.review: Arriving before check-in or leaving after check-out? These lockers are on level -1 of Trindade metro station, so you can drop your bags and go. Handy if you're catching the metro to the airport later: it leaves from the same station.

places.name: Locker in the City
places.review: A second option at Trindade, open around the clock. You book and pay online, then open the door and your locker with a code. Good backup when the metro lockers are full.

places.name: Luggage Storage Port
places.tagline: Staffed luggage storage on our street
places.review: The closest place to leave your bags: a couple of minutes up Rua do Almada from the house. Someone looks after them in person.

places.name: Lavandaria do Almada
places.tagline: Self-service laundry, a minute from the house
places.review: Bright, clean and practical, right on our street. Washers and dryers are self-service and the detergent is included in the price, so you don't need to bring anything.

places.name: Clínica do Calçado
places.review: A broken heel, a sole coming loose, a strap or zip on your bag: this is the cobbler we trust. A small traditional workshop near Rua do Paraíso.

places.name: CC Bombarda
places.tagline: A small arcade of independent shops and designers
places.review: A small shopping arcade on Rua de Miguel Bombarda, full of local designers. Small shops with clothes, ceramics, prints and plants, and a nice stop between galleries.

places.name: Copo d'Uva
places.review: A well-chosen selection of Portuguese wines and good things to eat. The place to pick a bottle to take home, with honest advice.
places.address: Rua de Adolfo Casais Monteiro 101, Porto

places.name: Ó! Galeria
places.review: A gallery dedicated to illustration, with original drawings and prints by Portuguese and international artists. Affordable if you want to take some art home.

places.name: Tilsitt Gallery
places.review: A small contemporary art gallery on the art street, with changing exhibitions.

places.name: Galeria Fernando Santos
places.tagline: One of Porto's leading contemporary galleries
places.review: Painting, sculpture and installations in a large white space. One of the references of the Bombarda art scene.

neighbourhoodsIntro: Porto is small, but every part of it has its own character. This is a quick guide to the areas you'll hear about, from the old centre around the house out to the sea. Tap one to see it on the map.

neighbourhoods.name: Centro Histórico
neighbourhoods.tagline: The old city, a UNESCO World Heritage Site
neighbourhoods.intro: Steep granite streets, churches covered in azulejos and the Sé cathedral on its hill. The heart of old Porto, listed by UNESCO since 1996, and where most of the landmarks are. Best explored on foot, slowly, with no fixed plan.

neighbourhoods.name: Ribeira
neighbourhoods.intro: Colourful houses stacked above the Douro, terraces along the quay and the Dom Luís I bridge overhead. Busy with visitors, but at sunset it's hard to beat. Walk across the bridge to Gaia for the classic view back and the Port wine cellars.

neighbourhoods.name: Baixa
neighbourhoods.tagline: Downtown: Aliados, Bolhão and Santa Catarina
neighbourhoods.intro: Downtown Porto, where locals come to shop and meet. Avenida dos Aliados and the City Hall, the restored Bolhão market, the shopping street of Santa Catarina with the Majestic Café, and Trindade, the main metro hub. Lively by day, with cafés and bars on every corner.

neighbourhoods.name: Cedofeita
neighbourhoods.tagline: Creative Porto, a short walk from the house
neighbourhoods.intro: Galleries, independent shops, vintage and design stores, and some of the city's best new places to eat. Rua de Miguel Bombarda is the art street and Rua de Cedofeita the old shopping street.

neighbourhoods.name: Boavista
neighbourhoods.tagline: Avenues, music and the road to the sea
neighbourhoods.intro: Built around the Rotunda da Boavista and its long avenue to the ocean. Home to the Casa da Música, hotels and shopping centres. Follow the avenue west to reach Serralves and the Parque da Cidade.

neighbourhoods.name: Bonfim
neighbourhoods.intro: East of the centre, residential and still very local, with a new wave of cafés, restaurants and studios. Walk up to the Jardim de São Lázaro and the streets around Campo 24 de Agosto to see how Porto lives day to day.

neighbourhoods.name: Campanhã
neighbourhoods.tagline: The gateway, and a greener side of Porto
neighbourhoods.intro: Where the trains from Lisbon arrive. Beyond the station, the Parque Oriental and old farm estates show a quieter, greener Porto that few visitors see.

neighbourhoods.name: Foz
neighbourhoods.tagline: Where the river meets the sea
neighbourhoods.intro: The seaside end of Porto, running up the coast to Matosinhos. Walk the promenade past the Felgueiras lighthouse and the beaches to the Castelo do Queijo, have a drink facing the Atlantic and stay for the sunset. Tram 1 runs there along the river from near the Ribeira.

neighbourhoods.name: Foz Velha
neighbourhoods.intro: The original fishing village at the mouth of the Douro: narrow cobbled streets around the church of São João da Foz and the Passeio Alegre garden. Small restaurants, wine bars and old houses, a few steps from the sea.

neighbourhoods.name: Matosinhos
neighbourhoods.tagline: Beach town, and the best grilled fish
neighbourhoods.intro: Just north of Porto, with a long sandy beach, surf schools and Rua Heróis de França, lined with grills cooking fresh fish and seafood. Take the blue metro line, or walk along the seafront from Foz.

neighbourhoods.name: Afurada
neighbourhoods.tagline: A fishing village across the river
neighbourhoods.intro: On the Gaia side, a small fishing community where laundry still dries in the streets and sardines grill at the doors. Cross the Douro on the little ferry from Cais do Ouro, near Foz, and stay for lunch at one of the fish restaurants.

neighbourhoods.name: Canidelo
neighbourhoods.intro: Across the river in Gaia, just past Afurada. Sandy beaches like Lavadores, with rocky coves and a boardwalk along the coast, and sunset views back over Foz. Quieter than the Porto side.
